Medical Malpractice in Washington: The Standard of Care, the Deadline, and the Rules That Changed

Justin D. Leigh, Attorney-at-Law·8 min read·November 11, 2026

Your doctor felt the lump in March, said it was probably nothing, and did not order imaging. In November a different provider ordered a biopsy, and the cancer that might have been treated in March has spread. You have stopped trusting the clinic, and you want to know whether you can sue. In Washington the answer depends less on whether a mistake happened than on two things the statute makes you prove: that the care fell below what a reasonably prudent provider in that field would have done, and that the failure actually changed what happened to you.

Can I sue my doctor in Washington?

Yes, but not the way you would sue the driver who rear-ended you. Every claim for an injury caused by health care in Washington runs through chapter 7.70 RCW. RCW 7.70.010 says the chapter modifies certain substantive and procedural aspects of all civil actions for damages for injury occurring as a result of health care, "whether based on tort, contract, or otherwise." Calling it a breach of contract does not change that.

RCW 7.70.030 then limits the ways a patient can win. No award may be made unless the plaintiff establishes at least one of three propositions: that the injury resulted from a provider's failure to follow the accepted standard of care, that a provider promised the injury would not occur, or that the injury resulted from health care the patient did not consent to. The plaintiff carries the burden of proving each fact essential to an award by a preponderance of the evidence.

The statute reaches well beyond doctors. RCW 7.70.020 defines a health care provider to include licensed physicians, nurses, dentists, pharmacists, physician assistants, physical therapists, chiropractors, midwives and others, their employees and agents acting in the course of employment, and the entities that employ them, including hospitals, clinics, health maintenance organizations and nursing homes. A hospital negligence claim is brought under the same chapter.

What is the standard of care, and who decides whether it was met?

RCW 7.70.040(1) sets two elements. First, the provider "failed to exercise that degree of care, skill, and learning expected of a reasonably prudent health care provider at that time in the profession or class to which he or she belongs, in the state of Washington, acting in the same or similar circumstances." Second, that failure was a proximate cause of the injury.

"At that time" means the provider is measured against what was expected when the care was given, not against hindsight. "The profession or class to which he or she belongs" means a family physician is compared to family physicians and a surgeon to surgeons.

A jury does not know what a reasonably prudent radiologist does with an ambiguous image, so in practice these cases are built on testimony from qualified providers in the same field who have reviewed the records. That review is the first real step in any claim, and it is why these cases are slower and more expensive to start than most injury claims. For care given during the COVID-19 state of emergency, RCW 7.70.040(2) also lets the jury consider good faith reliance on government guidance and pandemic shortages.

Misdiagnosis and delayed diagnosis: proving it made a difference

A missed or late diagnosis is the claim people ask about most often, and the hardest part is usually not the mistake. It is the second element of RCW 7.70.040(1), proximate cause. The question is what would have happened if the condition had been caught on time, and whether the delay made the outcome worse.

That is a medical question answered with medical evidence: how fast this kind of condition progresses, what treatment was available at the earlier stage, and what the outcome would likely have been. A case where the diagnosis was late but the result would have been the same is a hard case, however clear the error. A case where the delay closed off a treatment that would have worked is a different case entirely.

Surgical errors and informed consent

A surgical error is usually a standard of care claim under RCW 7.70.040. Surgery on the wrong site, a nerve or organ damaged during a procedure, an instrument left behind, or a complication recognized too late are all measured against what a reasonably prudent surgeon would have done.

A separate claim exists when the procedure was done competently but you were never told what you were agreeing to. RCW 7.70.050(1) lists the elements: the provider failed to inform you of a material fact relating to the treatment, you consented without being aware of it, a reasonably prudent patient in similar circumstances would not have consented if informed, and the treatment proximately caused injury. Under subsection (2), a fact is material if a reasonably prudent person in the patient's position would attach significance to it in deciding whether to go ahead. Subsection (3) requires expert testimony to establish the material facts, which include the recognized serious risks and the recognized alternatives, nontreatment among them. In a genuine emergency where the patient cannot consent and no one authorized is available, subsection (4) implies consent.

How long do I have to file a medical malpractice claim in Washington?

RCW 4.16.350 sets the deadline, and it has three moving parts. The action must be commenced within three years of the act or omission, or within one year of when the patient or the patient's representative discovered or reasonably should have discovered that the injury was caused by it, whichever period expires later. In no event may it be commenced more than eight years after the act or omission.

The same section tolls the deadline on proof of fraud, intentional concealment, or the presence of a foreign body not intended to have a therapeutic or diagnostic purpose, until the patient has actual knowledge of it. From that date the patient has one year to sue.

The eight-year outer limit has a history. As the Washington Supreme Court recounted in Schroeder v. Weighall, 179 Wn.2d 566 (2014), the court had held the eight-year limit unconstitutional in 1998, and the Legislature reenacted it in 2006. The Legislature's statement of its reasons is printed in the notes to the section, and the current text says eight years.

Children are the hardest part of this section. RCW 4.16.350 still says that, notwithstanding RCW 4.16.190, a custodial parent's or guardian's knowledge is imputed to a person under eighteen. But in Schroeder the Supreme Court held that former RCW 4.16.190(2), which had eliminated the usual tolling for minors in medical malpractice cases, violated article I, section 12 of the Washington Constitution, and the current text of RCW 4.16.190, amended in 2023, no longer contains that exception. How those pieces fit together for a particular child is a question to put to a lawyer early, not one to assume your way through.

Do I need a certificate of merit or a notice before suing?

Older guides to Washington malpractice law describe a certificate of merit that had to be filed with the complaint, and some describe a waiting period after notice to the provider. Neither describes the statutes as they read today.

RCW 7.70.150, the section that required a certificate of merit, is no longer in the code. The Legislature's disposition table records it as repealed by 2023 c 102 s 10. The current text of RCW 7.70.100 contains no presuit notice requirement. What it requires instead is mediation: before a superior court trial, health care claims are subject to mandatory mediation, under procedures the statute directs the Supreme Court to adopt by rule, unless the case is subject to mandatory arbitration or the parties agreed after the claim arose to arbitrate it. RCW 7.70.120 adds that the mediation requirement may not be construed to abridge the right to a jury trial after an unsuccessful mediation.

What remains is a certification by the lawyer. Under RCW 7.70.160, the attorney who signs and files a claim under the chapter certifies that, after reasonable inquiry, it is not frivolous, is well grounded in fact, and is warranted by existing law or a good faith argument for changing it. That is the practical reason a lawyer will want the records reviewed before anything is filed.

My health insurance paid the bills. Does the jury hear about that?

In a malpractice case, it can. RCW 7.70.080 lets any party present evidence that the plaintiff has already been compensated for the injury from any source except the assets of the plaintiff, the plaintiff's representative, or the plaintiff's immediate family. If that evidence comes in, the plaintiff may show an obligation to repay the compensation and any amount paid to secure the right to it. Evidence of compensation by a defendant provider may be offered only by that provider.

So a health insurer's reimbursement claim and the premiums you paid need to be documented before trial, not discovered during it.

Where this goes wrong

The patient requests records only after deciding to sue, and finds that the chart is incomplete or that the imaging is held by a different facility entirely.

The three years is counted from the wrong date. RCW 4.16.350 runs from the act or omission, with the discovery year as an alternative, and both clocks need to be calculated at the start, along with the eight-year limit.

Somebody follows advice written before 2023 and chases requirements the current statutes no longer contain.

The claim is judged by how bad the outcome was rather than by whether the delay or the error changed it. A bad result alone is not a case.

A parent assumes a child's claim can wait until the child turns eighteen, and nobody calculates the deadline early, even though RCW 4.16.350 still carries a sentence imputing a parent's knowledge to a child.

The provider turns out to be a public entity, and nobody checks whether a claim has to be presented before suit. The article on claims against government entities covers that step.

What a lawyer does here

Most of the early work is getting the complete record and having it reviewed by someone qualified in the right field before anyone decides whether there is a claim. That means every chart, the images themselves and not just the reports, and the billing records, which often show what was ordered and when. It means identifying every provider and entity involved, and calculating both limitation periods and the eight-year limit on the first day, and checking whether a public entity is involved. And it means telling you honestly whether the standard of care and causation can both be proved, because a case that fails on either one should be identified before you spend a year on it.
